bands.why: The first row is the warm-up: the snake starts coiled around two critters, and a reasonable player clears the 7 x 8 board (1.00 measured).
The second row (one critter in the nest, five on the board, 27 moves) still goes to a reasonable player most of the time (0.86 measured).
The hardest row (8 x 10, seven critters hopping every move) is hard, yet a reasonable player wins about half (0.55 measured).
Random swipes rarely clear even the easiest board (0.07 measured): steering into loops is a skill.
An easy level takes a handful of loops, never a single move (median 15 measured).
A hard level uses most of its 34 moves (median 33 measured) and always ends within them.
An easy win scores the opening's three-critter loop plus the bonus for moves left (median 135 measured).

notes: Snare Snake after its design fix (design notes), four tuning rows sampled at their lower bounds (0/25/50/75), 100 seeds per cell. The toy's greedy bot caught 1 critter in 20,000 moves; with the snake starting coiled around a nest, critters that keep away and freeze beside the snake, loops that also catch the critters touching them, and a snake that grows, the greedy bot now catches its first critter within three moves in 99 % of the easiest runs and closes a loop catching more than one critter 1.2 times per easiest run (the kill test passes). Greedy wins 1.00/0.86/0.72/0.55 across the rows, random 0.07 of the easiest level and none of the others, lookahead 0.73 of the hardest. The first run had the second row at 0.92 (30 moves), only 0.08 below the warm-up row; 27 moves made the curve fall by 0.14, 0.14 and 0.17. Losses are almost all out of moves; a tangled snake is rare (2 to 9 % of random runs, none of the greedy ones). Status proposed until the owner's play-test (O6).
